paragraphs: What followed was utterly unexpected, and astonishing to Mitya. Even a minute earlier he could never have imagined that anyone would treat him, Mitya Karamazov, like this. Worst of all, there was something humiliating in it, and on their side something “supercilious and scornful.” Taking off his coat was nothing, but then he was asked to undress further. Or rather he was not asked but “commanded”; he understood that perfectly well. Out of pride and contempt he obeyed without a word. Several peasants had come in with the lawyers and stayed on the same side of the curtain. “They’re here in case force is needed,” thought Mitya, “and maybe for some other reason, too.”

“Well, do I have to take off my shirt, too?” he asked sharply, but Nikolay Parfenovitch did not answer. He was busy with the prosecutor, examining the coat, the trousers, the waistcoat and the cap, and it was obvious that both of them found the inspection very interesting. “They make no bones about it,” thought Mitya. “They don’t even keep up the most basic politeness.”
“I’m asking you for the second time—do I need to take off my shirt or not?” he said, even more sharply and irritably.
“Don’t trouble yourself. We’ll tell you what to do,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch. His voice was positively commanding, or so it seemed to Mitya.

Meanwhile the lawyers were holding a consultation in low voices. The coat, especially on the left side at the back, turned out to have a huge patch of blood, dry and still stiff. There were bloodstains on the trousers, too. What is more, Nikolay Parfenovitch, in front of the peasant witnesses, ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs and all the seams of the coat and trousers. He was obviously looking for something—money, of course. He didn’t even hide from Mitya his suspicion that Mitya was capable of sewing money into his clothes.

“He treats me not as an officer but as a thief,” Mitya muttered to himself. They shared their thoughts with each other with amazing frankness. The secretary, for instance, who was also behind the curtain, fussing about and listening, drew Nikolay Parfenovitch’s attention to the cap, which they were also feeling over.

“You remember Gridyenko, the copying-clerk,” the secretary remarked. “Last summer he was paid the wages for the whole office, and when he was drunk he pretended he’d lost the money. And where was it found? Why, in just such piping in his cap. The hundred-rouble notes were twisted into little rolls and sewn into the piping.”
Both lawyers remembered Gridyenko’s case perfectly well. So they set Mitya’s cap aside and decided that all his clothes would have to be examined more thoroughly later.
“Excuse me,” Nikolay Parfenovitch cried suddenly, noticing that the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was turned in and covered with blood. “Excuse me, what’s that, blood?”
“Yes,” Mitya jerked out.
“That is, what blood? ... And why is the cuff turned in?”
Mitya told him how the sleeve had got stained with blood while he was looking after Grigory, and how he had turned it inside when he washed his hands at Perhotin’s.
“You’ll have to take off your shirt, too. It’s very important as material evidence.”
Mitya turned red and flew into a rage.
“What, am I supposed to stay naked?” he shouted.
“Don’t get upset. We’ll arrange something. Meanwhile, take off your socks.”
“You’re not joking? Is that really necessary?” Mitya’s eyes flashed.
“We’re in no mood for joking,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered sternly.

“Well, if I have to—” muttered Mitya. Sitting down on the bed, he took off his socks. He felt unbearably awkward. Everyone else was clothed while he was naked. Strange to say, once he was undressed he felt somehow guilty in their presence. He was almost ready to believe himself that he was inferior to them, and that they now had every right to despise him.

“When everyone’s undressed, you somehow aren’t ashamed. But when you’re the only one undressed and everybody is looking, it’s degrading,” he kept repeating to himself, again and again. “It’s like a dream. I’ve sometimes dreamed of being in such degrading positions.” Taking off his socks was misery to him. They were very dirty, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see it. And what was worse, he disliked his feet. All his life he had thought both his big toes hideous. He particularly loathed the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they would all see it. Feeling intolerably ashamed made him, at once and on purpose, rougher. He pulled off his shirt himself.
“Do you want to look anywhere else, if you’re not ashamed to?”
“No, there’s no need to, for the present.”
“Well, am I to stay naked like this?” he added savagely.
“Yes, that can’t be helped for the time being.... Please sit down here for a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I’ll see to all this.”

All the things were shown to the witnesses. The report of the search was drawn up, and at last Nikolay Parfenovitch went out, and the clothes were carried out after him. Ippolit Kirillovitch went out, too. Mitya was left alone with the peasants, who stood in silence, never taking their eyes off him. Mitya wrapped himself in the quilt. He felt cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn’t pull the quilt far enough to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, “an insufferable time.” “He thinks of me as a puppy,” thought Mitya, gnashing his teeth. “That rotten prosecutor has gone, too. He’s contemptuous, no doubt. It disgusts him to see me naked!”

Mitya had imagined, however, that his clothes would be examined and then returned to him. So how furious he was when Nikolay Parfenovitch came back with completely different clothes, carried in behind him by a peasant!

“Here are clothes for you,” he said airily, seeming quite pleased with the success of his errand. “Mr. Kalganov has kindly provided these for this unusual emergency, along with a clean shirt. Luckily he had them all in his trunk. You can keep your own socks and underwear.”
Mitya flew into a fury.
“I won’t wear other people’s clothes!” he shouted menacingly. “Give me my own!”
“It’s impossible!”
“Give me my own. Damn Kalganov and his clothes, too!”

It was a long time before they could persuade him. But somehow they managed to calm him down. They impressed on him that his clothes, being stained with blood, had to be “included with the other material evidence,” and that they “did not even have the right to let him have them now ... taking into consideration the possible outcome of the case.” Mitya finally understood. He sank into gloomy silence and dressed hurriedly. He only remarked, as he put the clothes on, that they were much better than his old ones, and that he disliked “gaining by the change.” Besides, the coat was “ridiculously tight. Am I to be dressed up like a fool ... for your amusement?”
They urged him again that he was exaggerating, that Kalganov was only a little taller, so that only the trousers might be a bit too long. But the coat really was tight in the shoulders.
“Damn it all! I can hardly button it,” Mitya grumbled. “Please tell Mr. Kalganov from me that I didn’t ask for his clothes, and it’s not my doing that they’ve dressed me up like a clown.”
“He understands that, and he’s sorry ... I mean, not sorry to lend you his clothes, but sorry about all this business,” mumbled Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Confound his sorrow! Well, where now? Am I to go on sitting here?”

He was asked to go back to the “other room.” Mitya went in, scowling with anger and trying not to look at anyone. Dressed in another man’s clothes, he felt disgraced, even in the eyes of the peasants and of Trifon Borissovitch, whose face appeared in the doorway for some reason and vanished at once. “He’s come to look at me dressed up,” thought Mitya. He sat down on the same chair as before. He had an absurd, nightmarish feeling, as though he were out of his mind.

“Well, what now? Are you going to flog me? That’s all you have left,” he said, clenching his teeth and addressing the prosecutor. He would not turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as though he disdained to speak to him.
“He looked too closely at my socks, and turned them inside out on purpose to show everyone how dirty they were—the scoundrel!”
“Well, now we must proceed to the examination of witnesses,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, as though answering Mitya’s question.
“Yes,” said the prosecutor thoughtfully, as though he were reflecting on something.

“We’ve done what we could in your interest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on. “But you have flatly refused to explain to us where you got the money found on you. So at the present moment we are—”
“What’s the stone in your ring?” Mitya interrupted suddenly, as though waking from a daydream. He pointed to one of the three large rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s right hand.
“Ring?” Nikolay Parfenovitch repeated in surprise.
“Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins in it. What stone is that?” Mitya persisted, like a peevish child.
“That’s a smoky topaz,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch with a smile. “Would you like to look at it? I’ll take it off ...”

“No, don’t take it off,” cried Mitya furiously, suddenly coming to himself and angry with himself. “Don’t take it off ... there’s no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you’ve dirtied my heart! Can you imagine that I’d hide it from you, if I had really killed my father? That I’d dodge, and lie, and hide myself? No, that’s not like Dmitri Karamazov. He couldn’t do it. And if I were guilty, I swear I wouldn’t have waited for you to come, or for the sunrise as I first meant to. I’d have killed myself before now, without waiting for the dawn! I know that about myself now. I couldn’t have learned so much in twenty years as I’ve found out in this accursed night!... And would I be like this on this night, at this moment, sitting here with you? Could I talk like this, could I move like this, could I look at you and at the world like this, if I had really been my father’s murderer? When even the thought of having accidentally killed Grigory gave me no peace all night—not from fear—oh, not simply from fear of your punishment! The disgrace of it! And you expect me to be open with scoffers like you, who see nothing and believe in nothing, blind moles and scoffers, and to tell you about another nasty thing I’ve done, another disgrace, even if that would save me from your accusation! No, better Siberia! The man who opened the door to my father and went in at that door, he killed him, he robbed him. Who was he? I’m racking my brains and I can’t think who. But I can tell you it was not Dmitri Karamazov, and that’s all I can tell you, and that’s enough, enough, leave me alone.... Exile me, punish me, but don’t bother me any more. I won’t say another word. Call your witnesses!”

Mitya delivered his sudden monologue as though he were determined to keep absolutely silent from now on. The prosecutor watched him the whole time. Only when Mitya had finished did he remark, as though it were the most ordinary thing, with the most frigid and composed air:

“Oh, about the open door you spoke of just now. We may as well tell you, by the way, right now, of a very interesting piece of evidence, of the greatest importance both to you and to us, that Grigory has given us, the old man you wounded. When he recovered, he stated clearly and emphatically, in answer to our questions, the following. He came out onto the steps and heard a noise in the garden, and made up his mind to go in through the little gate, which stood open. Before he noticed you running in the dark from the open window where you saw your father, as you’ve already told us, Grigory glanced to the left. While noticing the open window, he observed at the same time, much nearer to him, the door standing wide open—that door which you have stated was shut the whole time you were in the garden. I won’t conceal from you that Grigory himself confidently affirms and bears witness that you must have run from that door. Of course, he did not see you do so with his own eyes, since he first noticed you only some distance away in the garden, running towards the fence.”
Mitya had leapt up from his chair halfway through this speech.
“Nonsense!” he yelled in a sudden frenzy. “It’s a barefaced lie. He couldn’t have seen the door open because it was shut. He’s lying!”
“I consider it my duty to repeat that he is firm in his statement. He does not waver. He sticks to it. We’ve cross-examined him several times.”
“Precisely. I have cross-examined him several times,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed warmly.

“It’s false, false! Either someone’s trying to slander me, or it’s the hallucination of a madman,” Mitya still shouted. “He’s simply raving, from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it when he came to.... He’s raving.”
“Yes, but he noticed the open door not when he came to after his injuries, but before that, as soon as he went into the garden from the lodge.”
“But it’s false, it’s false! It can’t be so! He’s slandering me out of spite.... He couldn’t have seen it ... I didn’t come from the door,” gasped Mitya.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and said to him impressively:
“Confront him with it.”
“Do you recognize this object?”
Nikolay Parfenovitch laid a large, thick official envelope on the table. Three seals still remained intact on it. The envelope was empty, slit open at one end. Mitya stared at it with wide eyes.

“It ... it must be my father’s envelope, the envelope that held the three thousand roubles ... and if it says on it, allow me, ‘For my little chicken’ ... yes—three thousand!” he shouted. “Do you see, three thousand, do you see?”
“Of course we see. But we didn’t find the money in it. It was empty, lying on the floor by the bed, behind the screen.”
For some seconds Mitya stood as though thunderstruck.

“Gentlemen, it’s Smerdyakov!” he shouted suddenly at the top of his voice. “He’s the one who murdered him! He robbed him! No one else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It’s Smerdyakov, that’s clear now!”
“But you, too, knew of the envelope and that it was under the pillow.”

“I never knew it. I’ve never seen it. This is the first time I’ve looked at it. I’d only heard of it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden, I didn’t know ...” Mitya was completely breathless.
“But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father’s pillow. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known it.”
“We’ve got it written down,” confirmed Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“Nonsense! It’s absurd! I had no idea it was under the pillow. And maybe it wasn’t under the pillow at all.... It was just a chance guess that it was under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Have you asked him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say? That’s the chief point.... And I went out of my way to tell lies against myself.... I said without thinking that it was under the pillow, and now you— Oh, you know how one says the wrong thing without meaning to. No one knew but Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, and no one else.... He didn’t even tell me where it was! But it’s his doing, his doing; there’s no doubt about it. He murdered him, that’s as clear as daylight now,” Mitya exclaimed more and more frantically, repeating himself incoherently, growing more and more exasperated and excited. “You must understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and while Grigory was unconscious, that’s clear now.... He gave the signal and father opened to him ... because no one but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened the door....”

“But you’re forgetting the circumstance again,” the prosecutor observed, still speaking with the same restraint, though with a note of triumph, “that there was no need to give the signal if the door already stood open when you were there, while you were in the garden....”
“The door, the door,” muttered Mitya, and he stared speechless at the prosecutor. He sank back helpless in his chair. Everyone was silent.
“Yes, the door!... It’s a nightmare! God is against me!” he exclaimed, staring ahead in complete stupefaction.

“Come, you see,” the prosecutor went on with dignity, “you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On the one hand we have the evidence of the open door you ran out of, a fact which overwhelms you and us. On the other hand there is your incomprehensible, persistent and, so to speak, obdurate silence about where you got the money that was so suddenly seen in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own account, you pledged your pistols for the sake of ten roubles! In view of all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we depend on? And don’t accuse us of being ‘frigid, cynical, scoffing people’ who are incapable of believing in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to enter into our position ...”
Mitya was indescribably agitated. He turned pale.
“Very well!” he exclaimed suddenly. “I’ll tell you my secret. I’ll tell you where I got the money!... I’ll reveal my shame, so that I won’t have to blame myself or you later.”

“And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” put in Nikolay Parfenovitch, in a voice of almost pathetic delight, “every sincere and complete confession from you at this moment may later have an immense influence in your favor, and may, indeed, moreover—”
But the prosecutor gave him a slight shove under the table, and he checked himself in time. Mitya, it is true, had not heard him.
